results.title: QoS-Aware Irregular Collaborative Inference for Improving Throughput of DNN Services
results.venue: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis
results.abstract: With collaborative DNN inference, part of queries run on their source edge device to reduce latencies. Because edges show diverse performance and network conditions, different layers should run on different devices, and queries on the datacenter show irregular structures. However, emerging schemes are not able to process such irregular queries. We propose ICE, a collaborative inference service scheme that effectively supports irregular queries. ICE comprises a query slicer, a query manager, and a lag enhancer. The query slicer maps the execution of queries based on the edges' performance and network conditions. The query manager batches irregular queries adaptively and schedules the irregular queries based on their progress. The lag enhancer reduces the QoS violation when queries run slower due to interference on the edge. Experiments show that ICE improves the supported peak load of the datacenter by 43.2% on average while guaranteeing the required 99%-ile latencies compared with state-of-the-art techniques.

results.title: Task-Oriented Visual Feature Compression via Residual Vector Quantization for Device-Edge Multimodal Inference
results.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) support diverse visual understanding and reasoning tasks but are often impractical to run entirely on resource-constrained devices. Device-edge co-inference reduces device computation, yet transmitting visual data over bandwidth-limited uplinks can introduce substantial delay. Task-oriented feature compression (TOFC) reduces the payload through feature aggregation and entropy coding. However, continuous-feature coding remains costly, and query-agnostic aggregation may discard task-relevant local evidence. We propose query-guided task-oriented feature compression (Q-TOFC) for device-edge multimodal inference. Q-TOFC employs residual vector quantization (RVQ) to encode each merged feature as a compact sequence of codebook indices, reducing its representation cost and allowing more features to be transmitted. It further incorporates query relevance into feature aggregation and uses a quantization error compensation adapter to mitigate the distortion introduced by discrete quantization. Experiments on seven multimodal benchmarks show that Q-TOFC reduces the visual payload by 53.6% relative to TOFC while maintaining comparable average normalized task performance. End-to-end latency evaluations further demonstrate lower latency under bandwidth-constrained uplinks.

results.title: PW-Pruning: Phase-Aware Expert Selection for Speech-Centric Omni-Modal Models
results.abstract: Sparse routing reduces per-token computation but leaves the full expert bank resident in memory. We study expert pruning for speech-centric omni-modal models, where pooling calibration statistics can obscure the different expert demands of acoustic-input processing and text-answer generation. We propose PW-Pruning, a phase-aware extension of DO-ACP that constructs separate importance-weighted kernels for acoustic-prefill and teacher-forced answer tokens, then combines phase-weighted log-determinant marginal gains to select one static expert bank. On Qwen3-Omni, retaining 32 of 128 experts per layer improves MMAU-mini and MMSU accuracy over matched pooled selection by 3.20 and 4.38 percentage points, respectively, after supervised fine-tuning, averaged over three runs. Single-phase and shuffled-label controls on this public backbone suggest that semantic phase information contributes to these gains. Experiments on a non-public Qwen3.5-Omni backbone and English-only zero-shot evaluation of Nemotron provide complementary evidence. Across the tested Qwen budgets, AU gains are larger under stronger pruning, without inference-time mask switching.

results.title: TRIAGE: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference Needs Both Reuse and Pruning
results.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used for robot manipulation because they map camera images and a language instruction directly to actions. Robots that cannot be tethered to a workstation, such as mobile manipulators and humanoids, must run them on onboard embedded boards, where the prefill latency of the language backbone grows with the hundreds of visual tokens processed at every control step. To meet real-time limits, training-free accelerators recompute only a subset of the visual tokens and skip the rest, either by pruning them or by reusing their cached key-value (KV) states. The two options save nearly the same computation, yet existing methods apply only one of them to every skipped token. Through a token-level diagnostic, we show that which option keeps the action closer to full recomputation depends on the token's drift, the change in its shallow-layer value since its cache was computed. On both backbones tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4x the action error of pruning; the same diagnostic calibrates this threshold per backbone. Building on this finding, we propose TRIAGE, which deems a cache valid when its drift is below this threshold and it is not too old. TRIAGE recomputes a fixed budget of tokens, prioritizing important tokens with invalid caches, reuses every other token with a valid cache, and prunes the rest; prune-only and reuse-only methods are the two extremes of this partition. Because the budget fixes the number of recomputed tokens, it directly sets the prefill latency. On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation in average success rate while cutting prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%, and with only 7% of visual tokens recomputed, it beats the strongest baseline by 24.4 pp on LIBERO-Object.
